messages.subject: Re: MS1 Label Free Dataset
messages.body_plain:
Dear James,

Sorry for not answering sooner. Part of the reason for the silence is that we don't have a fully informed solution. The previous version of MSstats worked 'by accident' (i.e., we didn't do an extensive checking for such features, and therefore they were treated as if they were additional independent replicates - which is not quite the right thing to do).

For the time being, my advice is to use your best judgement. The important thing is to make sure that the same feature is consistently profiled in all runs, and the choice is independent from the intensity. (E.g., if you use the monoisotopic peak, use it consistently across runs. If you take the sum, take the sum of the same number of peaks across runs. Selecting the most intense peak in each run is incorrect, as it will bias the quantification). If you decide to separately use multiple such features, you will need to edit the dataset, e.g. add a character to the peptide sequence to provide a unique name.

We will also actively look into this on our side, and are hoping to provide a more informed and data-benchmarked solution in a longer term.

I hope that this helps at least somewhat
Sincerely
Olga

messages.subject: Re: Error - Group Comparison
messages.body_plain:
Dear Vendula,

You have a label-free experiment with 25 proteins, and from the number of proteins I assume that this is a targeted acquisition. Therefore your options for normalization are limited. Quantle normalization is not appropriate (it assumes that the number of proteins is large, and that the majority of the quantified proteins do not change in abundance between conditions). Equalize medians is likely also not appropriate (it does not assume that the number of proteins is large, but assumes that at least 50% of the proteins do not change in abundance). The best approach in such an experiment is to include an internal standard ( a protein/peptide that is spiked in a constant concentration, or an endogenous protein that is known to be tightly regulated), and equalize the intensities of the standard between runs. This is the 'global standards' option.

Restricted scope of biological replicates means that your conclusions are restricted to the subjects selected for the study. Expanded scope of biological replicates means that your conclusions are expanded to the larger underlying populations of the subjects. The two approaches require slightly different models. The former is useful in screening experiments. It is more sensitive but less reproducible. The latter is useful in confirmation experiments. It is less sensitive but more reproducible. For details see http://www.biomedcentral.com/bmcbioinformatics/supplements/13/S16

HTH

Sincerely
Olga

messages.subject_clean: Setup for analyzing fractionated label-free data
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have been handed a set of in-gel digest data which we'd like to analyze via label-free quantification. Extracting intensities to use as input into MSstats is relatively straightforward, but my question is with regard to the input data matrix.
As I understand it, MSstats requires a line in the input data for every feature in every LC-MS/MS run. However for in-gel data we _expect_ most peptides to _not_ show up in a given run, due to the fractionation.

Is it more appropriate to input an extremely sparse data matrix to MSstats with NA for every run in which a peptide wasn't seen, or should the intensities be merged across runs beforehand in this case?

messages.subject: Re: Setup for analyzing fractionated label-free data
messages.subject_clean: Setup for analyzing fractionated label-free data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jason,

in your case, it is not necessary to have a row for every feature per run. Since each fraction (in principle) contains separate peptide or protein species, you only need to add rows with NA for the corresponding fraction. For example, if peptide1 appears in fraction3, you should have a row for each peptide in fraction3 of every sample (and NA for fraction3 of the samples where the peptide was not observed). You do not need to add rows in the other fractions.

An analogy is in targeted proteomics, where experiments may have more peptide targets than what can be acquired in a single run. Then the targets are split into multiple 'methods', and the peptide only needs all the rows in its own 'method'. The 'methods' can be thought of an an analogy for fractions. See section 2.1.1(i) of the user manual for more details.

HTH
Olga

Dear Vendula,

Sorry for this inconvenience. It seems that update didn't complete. We will check to make the error message for incomplete installation.
Temporary solution is to uninstall MSstats and reinstall MSstats. Please follow below,
1. Skyline > tool > external tool , then there are three function names (MSstats/QC, MSstats/groupComparison, MSstats/DSS). Please remove them, then click 'apply' at the bottom right.
2. Uninstall R 3.0.3 in control panel of your computer.
3. check whether the directory ,C:/Program files, has R folder or not. If you have, please remove the folder named 'R' under 'Profile files'
4. Then Skyline > tool > tool store, then install MSstats

, which will remove previous version 2.1.6 completely, then reinstall the newest version 2.3.4. If you still had error or difficulty, please let us know.

Thank you for reporting this issue.

Meena
